title: Medical Devices and MedTech
answer: The FDA keeps a public list of AI enabled medical devices it has authorized, now well over a thousand, most of them in radiology and most cleared through the 510(k) pathway. Its final guidance on predetermined change control plans lets makers get approval in advance for planned model updates, and in Europe AI devices also fall under the AI Act's high risk rules.

reading.body:
The FDA's list of authorized AI medical devices has passed a thousand, and the approval regime now has a mechanism for updating models without starting over.

The pattern is regulatory catch-up. Most of those authorizations are radiology tools cleared through 510(k), a pathway built for devices that do not change. Predetermined change control plans, finalized in December 2024 and widened from machine learning devices to all AI enabled devices, let a maker get advance approval for planned model updates. That matters because retraining is continuous and a fresh submission per version is not viable. In Europe the same device must satisfy MDR or IVDR and, since August 2024, the AI Act, which classes devices needing notified body review as high risk.

For AI specifically, the constraint is not the model but the permission to change it. A device that cannot be updated decays in place, and the compute behind it is irrelevant if the update cannot be cleared. The practical consequence is that change control gets designed at first submission, not after.

What this does not cover: the data gives no counts by year, no breakdown beyond radiology's majority, no recall or post-market outcomes, and no detail on how generative or large language model devices are treated. It also says nothing about compute, data centers, or power, which do not appear in this material at all.

Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.

The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.

A set of step-by-step rules or instructions a computer follows to solve a problem or perform a calculation. In machine learning the algorithm is the recipe for learning from data; the model is what the recipe produces.

explainer:
Medical devices include software as well as hardware. An algorithm that reads a scan, flags an irregular heartbeat or estimates a risk score can itself be a regulated device, known as software as a medical device. That makes medtech the part of life sciences where AI has been authorised for clinical use the longest and in the largest numbers.

In the United States most AI devices reach the market through the 510(k) pathway, by showing they are substantially equivalent to a device already cleared. Genuinely new moderate risk devices use the De Novo route, and high risk devices need premarket approval with clinical evidence. Radiology accounts for most authorisations so far, because imaging produces large labelled datasets and well defined tasks.

AI raises a problem the device rules were not built for: models can be retrained and improved after launch. The FDA's answer is the predetermined change control plan, which lets a maker agree in advance which changes it will make and how it will validate them. Europe applies its medical device regulations and, on top, the AI Act's requirements for high risk systems.

Generative AI is the open frontier. Devices built on large language models produce variable outputs that are hard to test exhaustively, and regulators are still consulting on how to authorise them.
key_points: AI software can itself be a regulated medical device.
Most US AI devices are cleared through 510(k); radiology dominates.
Predetermined change control plans allow planned model updates without new submissions.
EU AI devices must meet both MDR or IVDR and the AI Act.
Generative AI devices do not yet have a settled pathway.
